en: Keśava: *Sāṃkhyatattvapradīpikā* (or *Sāṃkhyārthatattvapradīpikā*). Om! Salutation to the Supreme Self. *Sāṃkhyatattvapradīpikā*.
I take refuge in her who is most capable of warding off the mental anguish that is so difficult to restrain, and who generates a mass of joy for the world. (1)
The wise Keśava, son of Sadānanda, who was born of Bhaṭṭa Keśava and is a knower of the Yajurveda, has spoken something on Sāṃkhya according to his understanding. (2)
In this system, reality is twofold: primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa).

Primordial nature alone is designated as the "primal substance" (pradhāna); its definition as the essential nature of prakṛti is that it consists of the three qualities (guṇas), beginning with sattva, and is eternal.
Furthermore, because it is devoid of transformation, it is indeed eternal.
The term "consisting of the three qualities, such as *sattva*" (*sattvāditriguṇā*) is stated in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the *puruṣa*.
The analysis of the compound is: "that which has the three qualities, *sattva* and so forth.
The term "eternal" (*nityā*) is used to prevent over-extension to the principles (*tattva*) beginning with *mahat*, since these too are composed of the three qualities.
The incidental definition (taṭasthalakṣaṇa), however, is that Nature (prakṛti) is the material cause of the universe.
For it is thus: the subject under dispute has pleasure, pain, and delusion as its general material cause, because its nature is invariably associated with them.

Whatever whose nature is invariably associated with something else has that [thing] as its general material cause, just as jars, bowls, and the like, whose natures are invariably associated with the general property of clay, have clay as their material cause.
For instance, a certain young woman produces pleasure in one lover, delusion in another, and aversion in yet another;
for what reason? Because, in relation to each of them respectively, there is the manifestation of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, which consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

And she [the intellect] is the first transformation of the twenty-fourfold *prakṛti*—that is to say, the modification known as the Great One (*mahat*), which is the very principle of the Great (*mahattattva*).

That which is designated as the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*) is the first modification of the principle of the Great One (*mahat-tattva*), known as the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) in the form of "I. Following that, there arise the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) called sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; then the five gross elements beginning with space; and finally the eleven organs—the eleven sense-faculties consisting of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose, speech, anus, genitals, hands, feet, and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

In this context, the seven principles—namely, the principle of Mahat (the Great One), the principle of Ahaṃkāra (the I-maker), and the five subtle elements (tanmātras) beginning with sound—are characterized by the relationship of both cause and effect. This means that each preceding principle is an effect with respect to its predecessor and a cause with respect to each subsequent one. To illustrate: the principle of Mahat is the effect of the Root Nature (Mūlaprakṛti) and the cause of the principle of Ahaṃkāra; the principle of Ahaṃkāra...

Likewise, the Mahat-tattva is both the effect and the cause with respect to the tanmātras known as the śabda-tattva and the others; for it should be understood that even these are effects with respect to what precedes them and causes with respect to what follows them.

Furthermore, the five elements beginning with space (ākāśa), along with the eleven organs—these sixteen evolutes—are produced solely from primordial nature (prakṛti) and are not themselves the nature (prakṛti) of anything else, because they lack the form of being the material cause (upādāna) of any other principle (tattva).
This primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is insentient because it is subject to transformation.

If it is asked: "Why should the connection of objects such as jars with consciousness not occur directly; why must it proceed through the channel of the *mahat* and so forth? [we reply: Would consciousness itself then have the inherent nature of being bound to objects? If that were the case, liberation could never occur, because consciousness would be eternal.

Now, if it is argued that consciousness is reflected in *prakṛti* and that there is a direct relationship between consciousness and its objects, making the intervention of the *mahat* and other evolutes unnecessary—then, since consciousness would be as eternal as the *puruṣa*, liberation could never occur.

Or, if it is argued that let consciousness not have the nature of being connected to objects, but rather let the objects themselves have the nature of being connected to consciousness; and thus, when the objects disappear, liberation occurs—then this would mean that "this is seen" could never happen, because there would be no mediation whatsoever due to the inherent nature of consciousness being connected [directly] to everything.

Now, if it is argued that objects, being connected to consciousness through the doors of the senses, may account for the practical distinctions between the perceived and the unperceived based on proximity and distance, we say no; for this would render the phenomenon of selective attention (vyāsaṅga) impossible, since the arising of cognition would necessarily occur whenever an object is connected to a sense organ. If it is then argued that the mind (manas) must be postulated because of the impossibility of such selective attention, what need is there for the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra)? Do not say so; for if that were the case, [the ego-sense would be required] in relation to itself...
One should not superimpose "I am a tiger" or "I am a boar"; rather, through the door of the mind, the intellect (citi) connected with it should grasp its own human nature.

Now, if it be argued that such an ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) exists for the purpose of superimposition during the state of dreaming, there is no evidence for this in the principle of the intellect (buddhitattva); do not say so, for [this is absent] in the state of deep sleep (suṣupti).

Just like the mind (*manas*), the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is also one whose activity has ceased; thus, there would be an activity of the life-force (*jīvanayoni*) effort which impels the breath. Since the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*) is likewise necessary to account for that [effort], the object—such as an elephant, a horse, or a buffalo—which is connected to the principle of intellect through its pervasion, becomes connected with the Person (*puruṣa*) through consciousness (*caitanya*). Therefore, liberation occurs precisely upon the destruction of the principle of intellect at the end of *saṃsāra*; thus, there is no lack of liberation.

The Puruṣa is without cause and without effect, having the nature of immutable consciousness; for by the Śruti, "In this regard, this Puruṣa is self-luminous," the self is declared to be self-manifesting.
And since self-manifesting is indeed consciousness itself, this Śruti, by declaring the self's state of being self-manifesting, makes known that the Puruṣa has consciousness as its essence.

Furthermore, it is not possible for momentary cognition to have the nature of an eternal self (*puruṣātmatva*), because the momentariness of cognition remains unproven; for your own theory, the conventional usage of "destruction" is justifiable as being merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), like the conventional usage of the destruction of space within a jar. Thus, even in your view—which accepts consciousness as distinct from the self—there is no evidence for the momentariness of cognition; otherwise, the recollection of what was experienced at another time would be impossible.

Nor is *saṃskāra* (latent impression) the door [to cognition], because it is simpler to assume the stability of cognition in relation to that assumption; and since it is eternal, it is neither a modification of anything nor a cause, owing to its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*). For if one were to resort to this [consciousness] as the primal nature (*prakṛti*) even though it is self-luminous, then either that which is intended to be its modification would also have to be self-luminous, or else this [consciousness] itself would become insentient (*jaḍa*), for [the relationship of cause and effect] applies only between two things of the same nature.

Because the relationship between primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and its transformations (*vikṛti*) is perceived, and because their distinction is not grasped, the Puruṣa—though devoid of action—possesses the conceit of agency; likewise, the empirical usage of pleasure, pain, and so forth occurs in this manner. For the Puruṣa, whose form is pure consciousness, who stands aloof from the state of being either nature or its transformation, and who is untainted like a lotus leaf, nevertheless, through ignorance (*avidyā*) characterized by non-discrimination, enters into identity with Nature as it has transformed into the form of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Consequently, due to mutual superimposition (*adhyāsa*), there arises the empirical usage such as "I am suffering," because the modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—such as pain and so forth—are superimposed upon the Self (*puruṣa*), and the attributes of the Self—such as pure consciousness (*cit-caitanya*) and so forth—are superimposed upon the internal organ.

This appearance of non-discrimination (*avidyā*) is not ultimately real; arising from the predominance of the quality of darkness (*tamas*), it manifests the identity of two things that are actually distinct.
Furthermore, ignorance is proclaimed to be the cause of the higher afflictions—namely, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the clinging to life—which are designated by the term "kleśa.
Thus it is established that this [Self] is indeed untainted;
and this is also logically supported by the Vedic scripture: "For this is unattached."

Furthermore, there is no activity whatsoever belonging to the Self (*ātman*). To explain: first, "observation" (*ālocana*) is the activity of the sense organs; "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*) is that of the mind (*manas*); "self-conceit" (*abhimāna*) is that of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*); and "determination of action" (*kṛtyadhyavasāya*) is that of the intellect (*buddhi*).

Now, if the determination of action is knowledge by virtue of possessing activity (*kṛtimattā*), how can it belong to the insentient intellect? The intellect possesses three aspects: the reflection of the Person (*puruṣoparāga*), the reflection of the object (*viṣayoparāga*), and the penetration of activity (*vyāpārāveśa*).
For indeed, one thinks, "This must be done by me. In this context, the aspect "by me" belongs to the conscious [Self], while the intellect is as stainless as a mirror.

The reflection is a superimposition (*upadhāna*), and it is indeed unreal because there is no real connection between consciousness (*caitanya*) and the intellect (*buddhi*); just as there is the delusion of a person [in a mirror] even without a connection between the mirror and the face, so it is here as well.
The "this" is the superimposition of the object, and that is real because of the connection between the object and the form of cognition in the intellect through the channel of the sense organ.

Just as the impurity of a mirror struck by breath is not its ultimate nature, so too the Puruṣa’s coloring by objects is not its ultimate nature; rather, the determination of its agency through the power of the coloring by objects is precisely this "entry into activity. Now, if consciousness itself is sentience, how can there be a distinction between these two? It is said: [the Puruṣa] is characterized by the activity consisting of the determination of action.

The intellect (buddhi) possesses a specific modification (vṛtti-viśeṣa), which is the connection between the intellect and its object, such as a jar, through the channel of the sense organs; that itself is cognition (jñāna).
That which is the unreal (atāttvika) connection of the Puruṣa with the coloring (uparāga) by the object is apprehension (upalabdhi);
the meaning is that it is just as the impurity residing in a mirror is seen on the face reflected in that mirror.
Likewise, it should be understood that the apprehension known as *anuvyavasāya*—expressed as "I know the jar"—is [itself] cognition.

Furthermore, the eight states (*bhāva*) consisting of pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit (*dharma*), and demerit (*adharma*) belong to the intellect (*buddhi*) alone, because of the perceived coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in cognitions such as "I know" and "I am happy.

If it is objected: "Why should that which possesses these attributes not itself be the conscious entity? We say no, because it undergoes transformation (*pariṇāmin*) by virtue of having impermanent attributes, and because there is no difference between an attribute and its substratum (*dharmadharmiṇor abhedāt*).

Furthermore, those such as the logicians (*tārkika*) who maintain a distinction between these two [the Self and the intellect] are to be disregarded, for they do not perceive the cognition that apprehends non-difference, such as "this is a blue jar.

Now, one might object: how can the Pradhāna, being insentient (*acetana*), be the creator of the world? For whatever is manifested through name and form is seen to have a sentient creator, just like a jar or similar objects. And the world under dispute is manifested through name and form; therefore, it is probable that it has a sentient creator. Thus, [the opponent suggests] a sentient being [is the cause].
For indeed, having delineated name-and-form within the intellect, one produces an external jar through the name "jar" and through its form, such as the neck shaped like a conch-shell and so forth.

For this very reason, even though the jar is that which is to be produced, it possesses the status of an object and an agent because it is established within the intellect as a mental construct; thus, one says, "he makes a jar.
To this we reply: if consciousness were the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, the insentience of the world would be untenable, for whatever is an effect has a conscious agent.

By the pervasion [of the rule] that "the embodied one is the agent," [one might argue for an agent]; yet even so, there is no evidence for the fact that consciousness—characterized by sentience—is the producer of the earth and other elements, because the cognitions and desires of potters and others are otherwise accounted for as being produced solely by their volitional efforts (*kṛti*), and because God’s own volitional effort must itself be produced.

If it is argued that its existence is established by the pervasion that "whoever possesses volitional effort possesses cognition," then by the pervasion that "whoever possesses cognition is happy," happiness would also belong to God; and if you claim this is an unproven reason (*aprayojakatva*), that applies equally to your position as well.

Even those who maintain that karma alone is the cause of the world are not to be entirely dismissed; for [karma] is characterized by injunctions (codanā) whose nature consists of merit and demerit, and which define what is beneficial and harmful, since there is no difference between [karma] and primordial matter (prakṛti).
This is because it is accepted that the eight states of being belong to primordial matter itself when it has transformed into the form of the intellect (buddhi).
Now, let us examine the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

That [means of valid cognition] is first of three kinds, distinguished as perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and scripture (*āgama*). Perception is the instrument for the production of perceptual valid cognition;
inference is the inferential mark (*liṅga*).

Now, how can there be the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*) for the past and the future? It exists because of their presence by way of their genus (*jāti*), which consists of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*). Verbal testimony (*śabda*) is authoritative speech, such as: "In this king's palace, there are elephants, chariots, and horses," as spoken by a traveler who has studied all [the relevant texts].
Since its purpose is already fulfilled by inference, analogy does not deserve to be a separate means of knowledge;
likewise, presumptive testimony, non-existence, probability,
and tradition are included therein, for that [tradition] is clearly nothing other than scripture, as is explained at length elsewhere.
Furthermore, this person is distinct in each body.
For instance: "The bodies under dispute possess selves numbering according to their own count, because they are bodies, like those [bodies] currently accepted as such.
Moreover, it is thus: just as when a single Devadatta is alive, or when his body is born, or when it possesses movement, or when it is dead—

Even when a living being possesses the capacity for movement, people conventionally say, "He is dead"; since such usage occurs identically even with respect to another body, one must therefore admit a distinction between persons.

Furthermore, because scriptural passages such as "One only, without a second" have their meaning applied figuratively in some way, and because the self is omnipresent, it is not distinct in terms of space and time.

Thus, they are spoken of as one; yet from such scriptural passages as, "For the one unborn [Self] lies down beside her while enjoying her, but another unborn [Self] abandons her once her enjoyment has been experienced," we understand the distinction between Puruṣas. What, then, is the purpose of this? It is the supreme good (niḥśreyasa). And what is that? It is the destruction of ignorance—which is the root of all misfortune—by means of knowledge manifested through a particular excellence of the quality of purity (sattva).
Upon the destruction [of the world], the persistence of that person (puruṣa) in the form of innate consciousness is the supreme good (niḥśreyasa), which is synonymous with liberation;
and the knowledge of the discrimination between primordial matter (prakṛti) and the person is its cause.

Now, one might object: since primordial matter is eternal, there is the possibility of a recurrence of the predominance of darkness (tamas), and thus, if ignorance (avidyā) were to manifest again, there would be a fall from liberation.
This is not so, because through the power of yoga—characterized by the cessation of the most firm mental fluctuations—a recurrence [of those fluctuations] is impossible.

As they say: "But that [yoga], when practiced for a long time, without interruption, and with devotion, becomes firmly established and is not overcome by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of worldly emergence. Now, it might be argued: "Since there is no connection at all with this stainless Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*), how can there be liberation? This is true; however, bondage and liberation actually belong to *prakṛti* alone, and are only metaphorically attributed to the Puruṣa. As they say: [text continues].
"Thus, by means of these seven forms, Nature binds herself by herself; and that same Nature liberates the Puruṣa from his purpose by means of a single form.
This is the meaning: dharma, adharma, non-attachment, attachment, power, lack of power, knowledge, and ignorance—these eight are the forms of Nature.

In this regard, primordial nature (prakṛti) binds itself by means of seven forms— such as merit (dharma), demerit (adharma), and so forth— which are distinct from knowledge, and it liberates itself by means of the single form called knowledge.
As they say:
"By means of dharma there is upward movement; by means of adharma there is downward movement.
Through knowledge there is liberation, while from its opposite, bondage is held to occur.
Thus, all that remains—flawless and established in the doctrine of the attainment of higher prosperity (abhyudaya)—is disregarded [here].
Homage again and again to Kapila, who has revealed the root of all that is harmful, who perceives the meaning of all principles of reality, and whose mind is filled with compassion.
Thus ends the Sāṃkhyārthatattvapradīpikā.
